questions.question: Electric current is defined as:
options: The rate of flow of charge — charge passing a point per unit time
The energy carried by each electron
The total charge stored in a battery

questions.question: 40 C of charge flows through a heater element in 8 s. The current is:
A torch bulb draws 0,3 A for 5 minutes. The charge that passes is:
options: 90 C — convert 5 minutes to 300 s, then Q = 0,3 × 300

questions.question: Conventional current is taken to flow:
options: From negative to positive outside the battery, like the electrons
From the positive terminal through the external circuit to the negative terminal

subtopics.title: Potential Difference, Emf and the Volt

questions.question: One volt is equivalent to:
36 J of work moves 6 C of charge through a resistor. The potential difference across it is:
Pushing 4 C through a 12 V system transfers:
The emf of a battery is the reading across its terminals:
options: While it delivers its maximum current
Only when the battery is flat
When no current flows — the open-circuit energy promise per coulomb

subtopics.title: Ammeters and Voltmeters — Reading the Circuit

questions.question: An ammeter is connected:
options: In series, so every coulomb it counts passes through it

questions.question: An ideal voltmeter has:
options: Very high resistance, so it steals almost no current through its parallel path
The same resistance as the component
Very low resistance, to let current through easily

questions.question: A voltmeter wrongly wired in series will:
options: Throttle the current to almost nothing with its huge resistance — the circuit stops working

questions.question: An ammeter wrongly wired in parallel is dangerous because:
options: It reads volts instead of amperes
It blocks the main path completely
Its near-zero resistance invites a huge current — a short circuit

subtopics.title: Resistance — the Friction of the Wire

questions.question: Microscopically, resistance arises because:
options: Free electrons repeatedly collide with the vibrating ions of the metal lattice, transferring energy as heat
Electrons run out of charge along the wire

questions.question: Doubling the length of a wire:
options: Doubles its resistance — more lattice to cross, more collisions

questions.question: Making a wire thicker:
options: Decreases its resistance — more parallel lanes of travel

questions.question: Heating elements are wound in nichrome rather than copper because nichrome:
options: Resists strongly, converting electrical energy to heat on purpose

subtopics.title: The Water Pump on the Roof

questions.question: In the water-feature picture, the battery is the pump because it:
options: Loads every coulomb with a parcel of energy before sending it around
Consumes the water on each lap

questions.question: A battery goes flat because:
options: Its charge has all leaked away
Its chemical lifting power gives out — the charge itself is never consumed
The electrons in it get used up

questions.question: A battery under load reads slightly below its shelf reading because:
options: The voltmeter is broken under load
The emf falls when the shop light is on
Internal resistance spends some energy inside the battery — the delivery sits below the promise

questions.question: In the turnstile picture, current corresponds to:
options: How many supporters click through the gate each second

questions.question: The current on the two sides of a glowing bulb is:
options: Identical — charge is never used up; the bulb takes only the energy it carries
Smaller on the far side, because the bulb consumed some

questions.question: In a metal wire, the particles that actually drift are:
options: Positive ions, moving with the arrow
Electrons, drifting opposite to the conventional-current arrow
Protons, moving toward the negative terminal

questions.question: In the corridor picture, the heat generated in a resistor corresponds to:
options: The jostling left in the crowd by every bump as you push through
The speed of the fastest learner
The number of doors along the corridor

questions.question: The combination giving MAXIMUM resistance is a wire that is:
A hot metal wire resists more than a cold one because:
options: Heat adds extra electrons to the wire
The wire becomes longer when hot
Electrons move too fast to collide
The heated ions rattle harder, so electrons collide with them more often
